newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian markets shrug off Lebed sacking.
newsitem.headline: Russian markets shrug off Lebed sacking.

text.p: Russian financial markets on Friday shrugged off President Boris Yeltsin's dramatic sacking of security chief Alexander Lebed and investors focused more on economic factors, both good and bad.
Most leading shares rose modestly, confounding forecasts of a drop in prices, and Ministry of Finance bonds, or Minfins, rose on buying by Russian and Western clients.

"Investors who are here for the long term are a lot more willing to take these intermittent bumps and Lebed was never really a friend of the business community," said senior equity analyst Tad Berger of Creditanstalt-Grant.
"We are not seeing a lot of sell-side activity right now."

Berger said Russia's recent credit rating for its planned Eurobond, the international stock issue for gas monopoly Gazprom and Russia's inclusion in emerging market stock indices could help drive prices higher in coming weeks.
"I would think we would be stable to slightly up, because we are going to see any negative impact today and next week that should be discounted," he added.
Gazprom is seeking $460 million with an issue of American Depositary Shares and market talk is of keen investor interest.
Berger noted that shares, which soared in the run-up to the July presidential election run-off before falling on concern over Yeltsin's health, had not regained pre-election levels.
Renaissance Capital trader Victor Pitaleff said there was little buying but investors were neutral on Lebed's dismissal.

"A lot of people in Moscow think Lebed is very popular with the people and that he could create quite a stir but it doesn't look as if that is going to happen," he said. "The market is more or less resilient, considering all the news and rumours."
Sberbank dealer Pavel Sool said Minfin prices rose on rumours that details of Russia's Eurobond could be released on Friday and not on any reaction to Lebed.
"We received many calls from London and they didn't know how to understand this news," he said.
But markets could be in for another test of nerve in coming weeks as the government struggles to push its 1997 draft budget through parliament.
The State Duma, the lower house, rejected the draft on Wednesday, highlighting what it considered unrealistic revenue targets, and told the government to rethink its spending plans.

Concern over budget revenues led the International Monetary Fund to delay payment earlier this year of a tranche of a $10 billion loan to Russia. An IMF mission is in Moscow to assess whether to pay the latest tranche.
Analysts have also said market nervousness is bound to increase as the date for Yeltsin's heart bypass operation, provisionally set for mid-November, approaches.
United City Bank fixed income analyst Andrei Yashchenko said Treasury Bill prices fell further on Friday.
"It was partly tied to news of Lebed's sacking but an even more important factor is the growing budget crisis and the danger the government might start to borrow aggressively," he said.
Yashchenko said the central bank's decision to cut its refinancing rate to 60 percent from 80 percent from Monday was a sign of its determination to drive yields down.
